studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the demand quoted here recurs throughout the surah in slightly different words each time. This version is the plainest of them, a request for something sent down from his Lord. The answer neither promises nor refuses, and the classical sources do not attach it to a specific episode, treating it as the standing form of the argument during those years.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb for answering a call, used in the Quran of God answering prayer as well. Here it is turned toward people, so responding to a call becomes the same act in both directions.
The plain verb for hearing, but the surrounding sentence gives it the weight of attending. Arabic uses the same word for sound reaching an ear and for a request being granted.
An active participle stating a present capacity rather than a promise to act. The wording concedes everything the objectors assume about power while declining the conclusion they draw from it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caller in that society had a defined role. Announcements were made by a man standing on a height or walking the lanes, and a summons to a meeting or a raid depended entirely on who answered it. Response was public and countable. To say that only those who hear respond described a mechanism everyone had watched: the crowd assembles from the people already listening.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the image of the dead not hearing more than once, and each time it stops short of saying that such people cannot be reached. The clause here about God raising the dead sits immediately after the comparison, so the sentence that describes an inability also names the one for whom it is not final.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes reception a condition rather than a result, which reorders how guidance is usually pictured. A message is not a force applied to an inert object; it meets something that is either open or shut. That places responsibility with the listener without making the speaker's work useless. And the mention of resurrection keeps the closure provisional, since the one who raises the dead is not bound by the present state of anyone.

crossReferences.why: States the same comparison plainly: the living and the dead are not alike, and graves cannot be made to hear.
Turns responding into an invitation: answer God and the Messenger when called to what gives life.
Repeats the limit exactly, that the dead and the turned-away deaf will not hear the call.

studies.applyIt: Pick a conversation today in which you usually prepare your answer while the other person is still talking. Do not prepare. Let a full second pass after they stop before you say anything. The passage makes hearing the condition of everything that follows it, and one second is enough to find out whether you were hearing.

studies.title: Communities Like Your Own
studies.meaning: Every creature that walks and every bird that flies is called a community, using the same word the Quran uses of human nations. The comparison is stated plainly and then left standing, and the commentators differ over how far it reaches: some read it of their being ordered and provided for as we are, others of their having their own forms of accountability. A claim about the record follows, and then a gathering that includes them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside a passage arguing with people who wanted a sign delivered on demand. The ayah answers by pointing at signs already present in enormous number. The surah belongs to the later Meccan years, when the exchange had settled into a pattern of demands and refusals, and much of its method is to redirect attention from the spectacular towards what is already in view.

keyTerms.note: From a verb for moving slowly along the ground. The word covers every walking animal and is used elsewhere of human beings too, so the category the ayah opens with already includes the listener.
The same word used of human peoples with their own messengers and appointed terms. Applying it to animals is the ayah's whole claim, and Arabic offers no gentler reading of the word.
The verb used of people driven together at the resurrection, taken from the herding of livestock and the mustering of armies. Here it is applied to the animals themselves rather than to their owners.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs lived closer to animals than to most people. A herder knew individual camels by temperament, tracked birds to find water, and read the movement of gazelles for weather. Poetry of the period describes ostriches and wild asses with a precision that only comes from watching them for hours. An audience like that would not have found animal societies a strange idea; they had watched the orders and hierarchies.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the bird flying with its two wings has drawn comment since the earliest period, because flight already implies wings. Classical commentators read the redundancy as a way of pinning the description to something actually seen rather than to birds as a category, holding the sentence to what is concrete.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah decentres the human being without demoting them. Other creatures are given the vocabulary of community and of gathering, which places them inside the moral architecture of the world rather than beside it as furniture. The middle clause makes a further claim, that nothing has been left out of the record, and the commentators differ over whether that record means this revelation or the preserved book of all things.

crossReferences.why: Says that birds in flight and all in the heavens each know their own prayer.
States that everything glorifies God, though people do not understand their praise.
Places the provision of every moving creature on God, in a nearby surah.

studies.applyIt: Watch one animal today for two full minutes: a bird on a wire, a cat crossing a wall, ants at a crack in the pavement. Do not photograph it. The ayah calls what you are looking at a community, and the claim only becomes interesting once you have watched long enough to notice that something is being organised.

studies.title: Deaf And Dumb In Darkness
studies.meaning: Three disabilities are stacked in one clause: unable to hear, unable to speak, and set in darkness, so that neither guidance nor a request for it can pass. Commentators note that the darkness is plural, matching the opening of the surah. The second half states that God leaves astray whom He wills and sets whom He wills on a straight path. The Quran holds this beside its constant address to human beings as responsible, and the classical tradition keeps both without collapsing either.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage arguing that the refusal on display is not an information problem. The surah is composed as a sustained case about revelation and its reception, and this ayah is one of its blunter statements. No occasion is reported. The people described had heard the recitation repeatedly and in some cases had defended it privately while opposing it in public.

keyTerms.note: The root also gives the word for something solid with no opening, like a rock with no crack in it. Deafness here is the quality of a sealed surface rather than a damaged organ.
Used of someone who cannot form words, and by extension of one who has nothing to say for himself. Pairing it with deafness closes both directions, so nothing enters and nothing is asked.
A broad open road rather than a track, borrowed into Arabic from a Latin word for a paved way. Its width matters: the image is not a narrow ledge but a road wide enough to walk without straining.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel in Arabia depended on hearing and speaking. A guide called directions back along a line of camels, and a party moving at night stayed together by voice. Losing the sound of the man ahead in the dark was how people disappeared. The three conditions in this ayah, put together, describe the exact situation that killed travellers, and every listener knew someone it had happened to.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the straight path here is one of a small number of terms in the Quran that linguists trace to Latin, arriving through Aramaic or Greek, from a word for a paved street. Its most famous appearance is in the opening surah, recited in every unit of the daily prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets divine will and human responsibility in the same sentence without resolving them into a formula, and the mainstream commentators treat the pairing as deliberate. Read with the rest of the surah, being left astray follows a settled refusal rather than preceding it. What the ayah rules out is a claim to have arrived on the road by one's own navigation, which is why the same book teaches its readers to ask for the path daily.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical three words for deaf, mute and blind, of those who bought error with guidance.
Turns the same road into a request, which is how the Quran teaches its readers to hold this ayah.
States the same double clause about leaving astray and guiding, right after mentioning clear speech.

studies.applyIt: In your next prayer, slow down on the line asking for the straight path and mean it as a request rather than a formula. You say it many times a day. Once today, put a specific decision behind it, something you are genuinely unsure about. The ayah describes people who cannot ask. Asking is the thing you still have.

studies.title: Whom Would You Call
studies.meaning: The question is put as a thought experiment and its force is in the last clause. Strip away everything comfortable, bring either punishment or the Hour, and ask honestly who you would call on. Commentators note that the appeal is to the questioner's own experience rather than to scripture or argument. The wording assumes the answer is already known to the people being asked, and the following ayah states it for them without waiting.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and addressed to people whose religion had a working division of labour: lesser powers for ordinary needs, and a high God behind them for emergencies. The Quran repeatedly points at that division as the weak point of the whole system. No specific occasion is attested here, and the argument is one the surah makes several times in different settings.

keyTerms.note: Literally a request to see, used as an invitation to imagine a case. This surah uses the form repeatedly to open arguments, turning each one into a question the listener answers internally.

The verb for calling out to someone by name, which gives the Quranic word for supplication. Prayer of this kind is described as address rather than ritual, so the question is about who you would shout for.

From the root for truth-telling, but applied here to consistency between claim and conduct. The condition attached to the question asks not for honesty in reply, but for a reply that matches how they actually behave.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sea travel from the Arabian coast was the standard emergency of that world, and the Quran returns to it often. A merchant on a Red Sea crossing in a storm had no options and no intermediaries. Traders who financed such voyages knew what the crews said when the wind turned, and it was not the name of a household idol. The question here relies on that common knowledge.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for calling on God in this ayah gives the ordinary word for supplication, and the Quran uses it for both prayer and shouting to a person out of earshot. The overlap is not accidental in the classical philology: the same act is being described, differing only in who is being called and how far away they are taken to be.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats crisis as a diagnostic rather than as a lesson. What a person reaches for when the arrangements fail is presented as the truth about what they actually believe, and everything calmer is treated as commentary on it. That is a claim about human nature the surah does not argue for; it simply invites the audience to consult their own memory, which is a stronger move than a proof.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same test at sea: they call God sincerely, and associate others once safely ashore.
Describes the same reversal, with those they call on failing them the moment the sea turns.
Narrates the storm, the vow made inside it, and the behaviour that follows deliverance.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the last time something frightened you badly, and remember the first words that came, before you had chosen any. Do not judge them. Just notice what they show about where you actually turn. Then, once today, turn there deliberately while nothing is wrong, so the reflex and the practice are pointed the same way.

studies.title: You Will Forget Them
studies.meaning: The answer to the previous question is supplied without waiting for a reply: it is Him you call. Then two conditions are attached. The relief comes if He wills, so the calling is not a mechanism, and afterwards you forget the rivals you had set up, which is offered as a description rather than a rebuke. The second ayah widens the pattern. Hardship was sent to earlier communities for a stated purpose, that they might turn and plead.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing an argument built on what the listeners already know about themselves. The reference to earlier communities draws on stories the audience had heard from traders and from the scriptural communities nearby. No occasion is reported for these two ayat. They sit inside a long passage that alternates between the Meccan present and the history of peoples who received messengers.

keyTerms.note: The verb for lifting a covering off something rather than destroying it. Distress is pictured as a cloth laid over a person, so relief is described as an unveiling of what was underneath all along.

A word for external affliction, often used of poverty, war and famine. It is paired here with a second term for bodily suffering, so the two together cover what comes from outside and what is felt within.

From a root for lowliness and for a child at the breast. The word describes the posture of someone with no leverage, asking rather than negotiating, which is exactly what hardship strips a person down to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Drought was the recurring affliction of Arabian life, and it produced a recognisable behaviour. Communities gathered, prayers were made in the open, and vows were pledged aloud about what would change when rain came. Then the rain came, and the season resumed. This cycle was familiar enough that the ayah can describe it in a clause and expect the audience to supply the rest.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for humble pleading appears only a handful of times in the Quran, and almost always in connection with hardship rather than with formal worship. Its root also produces a word for a suckling child. The vocabulary of asking is thereby tied to helplessness rather than to eloquence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hardship is given a purpose that is stated openly, and the purpose is relational rather than punitive: that they might turn and ask. That does not explain every affliction, and the Quran does not claim it does. What it establishes is that difficulty is not outside the arrangement. The forgetting described afterwards is the more sobering half, since it says relief itself can undo what the hardship began.

crossReferences.why: States the pattern as a rule: no town received a prophet without adversity coming, that they might plead.
Traces the forgetting in detail: he calls while lying on his side, then passes on as if he never called.
Shows the same reversal, with a blessing granted after distress and the earlier prayer set aside.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you badly wanted last year that has since arrived and stopped being remarkable to you. Name it out loud today, once, as the thing you were asking for. The passage describes forgetting as the ordinary aftermath of relief, and the only reliable repair for it is deliberately going back and looking.

studies.title: But Their Hearts Hardened
studies.meaning: The sentence opens as a wish that goes unfulfilled, which commentators read as expressing regret over an opportunity rather than surprise. Hardship arrived, and the expected softening did not follow. Two reasons are given, and they work together. Hearts hardened, which is a change in capacity, and their conduct was made to look good to them, which removes the sense that anything needed changing. Difficulty by itself is shown to be insufficient.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and part of the same passage about earlier communities that received messengers and were tested. The ayat around it describe a sequence rather than an incident: affliction, then no turning, then unexpected abundance. The classical sources do not attach this ayah to a specific people, and it is written to apply to the audience listening as much as to those it describes.

keyTerms.note: Used of stone and of dry ground that will not take water. The image is a surface that repels rather than absorbs, so the failure described is one of reception, not of understanding.
An intensive verb for adorning or decorating something. Nothing is added to the deed itself; only its appearance is worked on, which is why the person sees no reason to reconsider anything.
A word for force and for the hardship it produces, used in Arabic of both courage in battle and calamity endured. The single term covers the striking and the suffering that follows it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Farmers in the oases knew the difference between ground that took water and ground that had been left too long. Baked earth sheds a first rain entirely; the water runs off and the field looks watered without being watered. Everyone who had waited on a season understood that a downpour on hard ground was worse than useless, because it produced the appearance of relief.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the language of hardened hearts sparingly and always with a physical comparison in reach, usually stone or dry ground. It never treats the condition as permanent by nature. In another surah, the same passage that compares hearts to rock goes on to note that even rocks split open and let water through.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies a comfortable assumption, that suffering reliably improves people. It can, and it is sent with that possibility in view, but the outcome depends on the state of the one receiving it. The second cause named is subtler and more common: a settled account of yourself in which your conduct already looks acceptable. That account, once formed, makes every experience confirm it, including hardship.

crossReferences.why: Compares hardened hearts to rocks, then notes that some rocks split and release water.
Warns against hearts hardening as time lengthens, which is how the condition usually arrives.
Asks about the one whose bad conduct has been made to look good to him, so he considers it fine.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you do that you have stopped examining because you settled long ago that it is fine. A way you speak to someone, a corner you cut at work. Do not resolve to change it. Just describe it to yourself in plain words, without the reasons attached. The reasons are the decoration this ayah is talking about.

studies.title: The Gates Of Everything
studies.meaning: The most unsettling ayah in the sequence describes abundance as a stage of the process. Gates of every kind are opened, and the opening follows the forgetting rather than preceding it. Commentators describe this as being drawn out gradually, a giving that increases while nothing is corrected. The turn comes at the moment of delight, which is when the seizure is placed. The second ayah closes with praise, which the tradition reads as praise for justice arriving rather than satisfaction at ruin.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a prosperous trading city in a period of expanding wealth. Mecca's position on the caravan route and its role as a sanctuary had made a small number of families rich, and their prosperity was widely read as proof that their arrangements were sound. This passage takes the same prosperity and places it inside a different account of what it means.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for opening a door or a city, used across the Quran for granting and for conquest. Here it takes gates as its object, so provision is pictured as access rather than as a delivery.
A word for someone whose hope is cut and who has nothing left to say. It is the root behind one of the names for the devil, and it names dumbstruck ruin rather than grief.

The hindmost part of something, the tail of a retreating column. Cutting it names the removal of what would have continued, so the phrase describes the end of a line rather than the death of a generation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan fortunes turned on caravans, and a good year was visible: more animals, larger houses, more clients at a family's door. There was no separate language for luck and for blessing, so success at the market was read directly as approval from above. That reading was the city's confidence, and it is the exact assumption these two ayat take apart without ever denying that the wealth was given.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing their state at the moment of seizure shares its root with one of the Quranic names for the devil. Classical philologists connected the two through the sense of hope being cut off entirely. The same three letters therefore name a condition of speechless despair and a figure defined by exclusion from mercy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Abundance is separated from approval as firmly here as ruin was separated from bad luck earlier in the surah. Neither can be read as a verdict, which leaves a person without a way to score their own standing from the outside. That is unsettling and also freeing. The praise at the end places the whole sequence inside justice rather than inside anger, which is why the tradition treats it as an answer rather than a celebration.

crossReferences.why: Names the same gradual drawing out: they are led on by degrees, from where they do not perceive it.
Asks directly whether wealth and children extended to someone mean good is being hastened to them.
Warns against admiring another's wealth and children, and says what such things are actually for.

studies.applyIt: Notice a stretch of your life that is going unusually well and ask what you have quietly stopped examining during it. Ease removes pressure, and pressure is what most of us use for review. Pick one thing you would have checked in a harder year, and check it this week while nothing is forcing you to.

studies.title: If He Took Your Hearing
studies.meaning: The argument works by subtraction. Take away hearing, take away sight, seal the heart, and then ask who could give them back. The three are not chosen at random; they are the instruments the surah has been discussing, the means by which a message is received at all. Commentators note the escalation from senses to the organ of understanding. The closing comment turns from the audience to the manner of the Quran's own argument, which varies its approach and is still declined.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and one of a series of ayat in this surah that begin by asking the listener to consider a case. The people addressed accepted a supreme God above their other objects of worship. That concession is what the argument leans on: they would not have claimed that any lesser power could restore a sense once taken, and the ayah simply makes them notice it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for stamping a seal on a document or a container, closing it so nothing enters or is altered. It implies a completed act and an owner's mark, not a slow closing over time.

An intensive form meaning to turn something in different directions. Applied to the signs, it describes an argument presented from several angles rather than repeated, which is a claim about how the Quran is composed.
A less common verb for veering away from something, used of an animal shying from a path. The surah has already used two other words for turning away, and this is the third.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blindness and deafness were common and had no remedy. Eye disease spread in dust and heat, and a man who lost his sight moved permanently into dependence on his household. Everybody knew someone in that position. There was no physician to appeal to and no shrine that claimed to reverse it, so the question the ayah asks had a settled answer before it was asked.
studies.didYouKnow: Hearing, sight and heart appear together as a set more than ten times in the Quran, almost always in this order, and usually in connection with either thankfulness or accountability. The ordering is consistent enough that the classical commentators treated it as deliberate: two gateways, and then the place where what enters is dealt with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Gratitude is approached through the possibility of loss rather than through the pleasantness of having, which is a sharper instrument. A faculty you have never been without is invisible to you, and the ayah restores its visibility by removing it hypothetically. The move also carries an argument about worship: whatever cannot restore what it did not give has no claim on you, and the audience's own instincts already agree.

crossReferences.why: Names the same three gifts as given at birth to people who knew nothing, so that they might be thankful.
Repeats the trio and notes how little thanks follows from having been given them.
Places the same set at the completion of the human being, after the shaping of the body.

studies.applyIt: Close your eyes for sixty seconds somewhere you would normally be looking around, and try to keep track of what is happening near you. Then open them. This ayah works by subtraction, and the demonstration takes a minute. Most people find the return of ordinary sight is briefly, unmistakably, a gift rather than a fact.

studies.title: Bearers Of Good News
studies.meaning: The question narrows what punishment would mean if it came, whether by surprise or in plain view: only the wrongdoing would be destroyed. Then the job description of a messenger is given in two words, good news and warning, in that order. Commentators note that the good news is stated first and that the condition attached is doubled. Those who believe and put things right are the ones described, and what is promised them is the absence of two specific things, fear ahead and grief behind.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a sequence of ayat that answer demands to see the punishment the recitation kept mentioning. The community around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was small and under pressure, and the promise here is addressed to them as much as the question is addressed to their opponents. No occasion is reported for these two ayat in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: Arrival with no approach visible beforehand. Paired here with its opposite, openly, the two words together close off every manner in which such a thing could come.
From a root for skin, since news shows first in the face. The word names a messenger by the effect he produces, and its placement before the word for warner sets the order of the work.
A verb for repairing what is broken, used of mending a wall, a quarrel or a life. Set beside believing, it makes the second half of the condition practical and outward facing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man who brought good news to a household was given something for it, by custom, and the gift had its own name. He came ahead of the caravan to say that the goods and the men were safe. Arriving with bad news was a different role entirely, often given to someone senior enough to absorb the reaction. Both messengers were familiar figures at a Meccan gate.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words describing a messenger's work here occur as a pair in more than a dozen places in the Quran, and the bearer of good news is named first in nearly all of them. The consistency is striking given how much of the surrounding material in those passages is warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pairing sets a limit on what a messenger is for. Neither man nor message is an instrument of force, which matches the surah's earlier point about angels and compulsion. The promise attached is worth reading precisely. It removes fear about what is coming and grief about what is gone, which are the two directions in which a mind travels when it is unsettled, and leaves the present untouched and unpromised.

crossReferences.why: Gives the reason for sending messengers with news and warning: so that no argument remains against God.
Attaches the same freedom from fear and grief to those who say God is their Lord and then stay upright.
Applies the identical phrase to the close friends of God, in another Meccan setting.

studies.applyIt: Write down the two things currently taking most of your attention: one you are dreading and one you regret. Look at the pair. The promise in this ayah is aimed at exactly those two directions, and noticing how little of your worry sits in the actual present is a useful hour's work on its own.

studies.title: It Will Touch Them
studies.meaning: One short ayah balances the promise just given. The verb chosen for the punishment is unusually mild in its literal sense, meaning to touch or brush against, and commentators note the restraint. What follows is the reason, and it names conduct rather than opinion: they were stepping outside a boundary they knew was there. The word for that is not the word for disbelief used earlier, so denial and defiance are being distinguished in the same sentence that links them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the statement that those who believe and set things right have nothing to fear. The two ayat are a matched pair, and the surah frequently works this way, placing a promise and its counterpart back to back. No occasion is attested. The audience included men who had heard the recitation for years and had made their position public.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for physical contact, weaker than striking or seizing. Its use for punishment is deliberate understatement, a device the Quran employs elsewhere when the reality being named is severe.
From a root describing a date breaking out of its skin. The picture is something leaving the covering that held it, so the failing named is stepping outside a known limit rather than not knowing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Boundaries in that world were real and marked. Grazing rights, water rights and the protected months around the sanctuary were all limits a man could see and could choose to cross, and crossing them was a public act with a name. Nobody stepped outside such a boundary in ignorance. The vocabulary of this ayah belongs to that setting, where a limit was known before it was broken.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for defiance here comes from a root that describes a ripe date pushing out of its skin, and the Arabic lexicographers preserved that literal sense alongside the moral one. The image is exact: something that belonged inside a covering emerging from it, still itself, but now outside where it was held.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Consequence is tied to a specific cause and stated with a light verb, which keeps the passage from reading as a threat delivered in anger. The distinction between denial and defiance also matters. A person is described here by what they did with a boundary they recognised, not by an inner state that only God can see, which is consistent with a book that repeatedly declines to sort people by their unspoken beliefs.

crossReferences.why: Matches the weight of a return to the act that earned it, evil repaid with its like.
States the same link between what hands earn and what befalls, while noting how much is pardoned.
Stands immediately before this ayah as its counterpart, promising the absence of fear and grief.

studies.applyIt: Think of a limit you know about and have been treating as flexible: a time you promised, a boundary someone asked you to keep. The word in this ayah is about stepping outside something you can see. Put yourself back inside that one line today, without announcing it to anyone, and notice how little it actually cost.

studies.title: I Do Not Say
studies.meaning: Three claims are refused in a row, and each was one the audience had either demanded or assumed: wealth beyond measure, knowledge of what is hidden, and angelic nature. What remains after the subtraction is stated in a single clause. He follows what is revealed to him. Commentators observe that the ayah defines prophethood by what it is not, and then closes with a question about the blind and the seeing that returns the burden of thought to the listener.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the demands being answered are recorded through the surah: a treasure to prove favour, foreknowledge to prove access, an angel to prove authority. The Prophet's ordinary circumstances were public knowledge in a small city, which is why an honest disclaimer was possible at all. The classical sources treat this as a general answer rather than a reply to one occasion.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a locked store where valuables are kept. It implies a keeper with access, which is the claim being declined, rather than wealth itself, which is what the audience heard.
What lies beyond perception, whether in the future or simply out of view. The word covers both, so the disclaimer refuses fortune-telling and hidden knowledge in one phrase.
A passive verb from a root for swift, quiet communication. The passive is the point: the one speaking is the recipient, not the source, which is exactly what the three refusals leave standing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had its diviners and its keepers of oracles, men consulted about lost camels, marriages and journeys, and paid for it. Their authority rested on claiming access to hidden knowledge. A man presenting himself with a message from God fitted that familiar slot, and the ayah refuses it explicitly, giving up the one role the city already had a place and a fee for.
studies.didYouKnow: Almost the same three-part disclaimer appears elsewhere in the Quran in the mouth of Noah, addressed to his own people. Two messengers separated by an immense stretch of time are given nearly identical words, which makes the refusal a feature of the office rather than a response to one situation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophethood is separated from power, from privileged information, and from a different order of being, leaving only the transmission of what is given. That protects the message from becoming a cult of the messenger, and it protects the messenger from claims he could not meet. The closing question adds the other half. Sight is not produced by argument, which is why the passage ends by asking for thought rather than assent.

crossReferences.why: Puts nearly the same threefold disclaimer in the mouth of Noah, answering his own community.
Extends the point: had he known the unseen, he would have secured good and avoided harm.
States that he is not unprecedented among messengers and does not know what will be done with him.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you are asked something and the honest answer is that you do not know. Say that, plainly, before you offer anything else. Most of us fill the gap with a guess delivered in a confident voice. This passage is a model of the alternative, and it costs less standing than you expect.

studies.title: No Protector Besides Him
studies.meaning: The instruction narrows the audience deliberately. Warn those who already fear being gathered before their Lord, which commentators read as identifying who the warning can actually reach rather than restricting who may hear it. The clause in the middle states the situation of everyone, not only the fearful: no protector and no intercessor apart from Him. The closing hope is expressed with a particle of possibility, so even the intended outcome is left open rather than guaranteed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage about who responds to a message and who does not. Mecca's religion assumed a chain of intermediaries, lesser powers who could speak on a person's behalf to the highest one. This ayah removes the chain in a single clause, and the argument recurs through the surah in different forms because it was the central point of disagreement.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb used of driving people together into an open space, as flocks or an army are assembled. The passive removes any choice about attending, which is what makes it something to be feared.

The relationship of a patron who stands behind someone in a dispute. In Arabian practice it was the difference between safety and exposure, so its denial here removes a specific social security, not an abstraction.

From a root meaning to make something even by pairing it. An intercessor joins himself to your case to strengthen it, which is why the Quran allows intercession only by permission rather than by influence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every serious matter in Mecca was approached through someone. A man seeking a settlement did not go directly; he sent a relative with standing, and the outcome depended on the weight of the person carrying the request. Access was the whole currency of the place. An arrangement with no intermediary available was not simply unfamiliar to that audience. It was structurally frightening.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for intercessor comes from a root meaning to make a pair, and it gives the Arabic for even numbers. Intercession is therefore pictured as adding a second to your one. The Quran never denies that this happens; it removes it from anyone's control by making it dependent on permission granted at the time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear here is treated as a capacity rather than a failing. Those who already sense that they will stand somewhere and answer are the ones a warning can reach, which makes a certain kind of unease a form of openness. The removal of intermediaries reorganises everything else. If nobody can be sent ahead on your behalf, the relationship stops being managed and becomes direct, which is harder and considerably simpler.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit for a day when no soul avails another and no intercession is accepted.
Answers the question of who holds intercession by assigning all of it to God alone.
Admits intercession while placing it entirely under permission, which is the balance this ayah assumes.

studies.applyIt: Think of a request you have been routing through someone else because approaching directly felt harder. Not every case can be changed. Pick one that can, and make the approach yourself this week. The passage describes a relationship with nobody in the middle, and practising that with people makes it less strange in prayer.

studies.title: Do Not Drive Them Away
studies.meaning: The people to be kept close are identified by one activity: calling on their Lord at both ends of the day, wanting His face. Nothing is said about their standing, and commentators note that this silence is the point. The middle clause removes the ground on which they could be judged, since their account is not his and his is not theirs. The final clause states plainly what dismissing them would amount to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical commentators report that leading men of the city offered to sit and listen on the condition that the poorer believers be sent away first, since they would not be seen among them. The reports name individuals differently and the sources vary in detail. What they agree on is the shape of the demand and the answer given to it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for chasing off an animal or turning someone out of a gathering. It is physical and slightly harsh, which measures exactly what was being requested behind the polite framing of the offer.
Used through the Quran for God Himself as the object of attention and the aim of an act. The idiom names what a person is actually after, which is why it appears where motive is being described.
The word for a tally of debts and credits. Placing it on both sides of the sentence, theirs and his, makes accountability strictly individual and closes off judging anyone by their circumstances.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan gatherings were arranged by rank. Where a man sat, who spoke first, and who was present at all were public statements about a family's standing, and being seen with the wrong company cost something real. Freed slaves and men without clans were at the bottom of that arrangement. Asking for them to be absent was not thought of as cruelty; it was ordinary etiquette.
studies.didYouKnow: A nearly identical instruction appears in surah 18, using the same phrase about calling on their Lord morning and evening and seeking His face, and adding that the eyes should not pass over them. Two surahs revealed in the same period preserve the same wording, which suggests a pressure that came up more than once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Access to a prophet is placed beyond the reach of social rank, and the reason given is not compassion but accounting. Nobody carries anyone else's record, so nobody's presence can be traded for anyone's approval. The passage also shows the cost of such a trade being named without softening. What was on offer was influence over powerful men, and the answer treats it as not worth the sentence that would have to be said afterwards.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the instruction almost word for word, adding that the eyes should not pass beyond them.
Records a related correction, where attention given to the influential cost attention owed to a seeker.
States the principle underneath: the measure of rank before God is care, not lineage or wealth.

studies.applyIt: Look at who you make time for this week and ask whether any of it is sorted by usefulness. Then give an unhurried twenty minutes to the person on that list who can do least for you. Not as charity. The passage is about who gets to sit in the room, and the answer it gives has nothing to do with what they bring.

studies.title: Are These The Ones
studies.meaning: The test described runs in both directions: some are tried by means of others. Commentators explain that the wealthy were tested by the poverty of those who believed first, and the poor by the scorn they met. The sentence quoted carries an unmistakable tone, asking whether these are the people God singled out. The answer is not an argument. It is a question about who is in a position to know, and the criterion it names is thankfulness rather than status.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the instruction not to dismiss the poorer believers. The early community drew heavily from people without clan protection, including freed slaves and men of small means, which the city's leadership found difficult to reconcile with a message claiming divine origin. The commentators treat this ayah as the general principle standing behind the specific instruction just given.

keyTerms.note: From a root for smelting metal to separate it from ore. The word covers both the fire and the sorting, so a trial in Arabic names a process with a result rather than an ordeal without one.
A verb for granting a favour freely. The same root produces the word for reproaching someone with a favour given, so Arabic keeps generosity and its abuse within one set of letters.
An active participle naming a settled quality rather than an act. Set against the sneer just quoted, it proposes a criterion that is invisible from outside and unaffected by what a person owns.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's hierarchy was visible in daily detail: who had clients, who walked with an escort, whose name was worth invoking at a market. A freed slave had no lineage to name and no protector to threaten anyone with. For men accustomed to reading rank instantly, the sight of such people being addressed as first among the guided was not a theological problem. It was a social absurdity.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran records this reaction in several places and puts nearly the same sentence in the mouths of much earlier peoples. In one passage the objection to Noah is that only the lowest among them follow him, phrased with the same disbelief. The complaint survives across the Quran's whole span of history unchanged in form.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes social difference itself the instrument of a test, which means the arrangement everyone is standing in is not incidental to their situation before God. Rank becomes a question rather than a fact. The criterion offered in reply is deliberately unverifiable by observers, so nobody can rank anybody by it, which removes the whole activity the sneer depends on.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle broadly: some are made a trial for others, and patience is asked for.
Records an earlier version of the sneer, that only the lowest among the people follow him.
Preserves the same reasoning: had it been any good, they would not have got there first.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you estimate someone quickly from what they are wearing or driving or doing for work. Everybody does this and it takes about a second. Once today, notice the estimate arriving and set it aside without replacing it with a better one. The ayah names a criterion you cannot see, which means the honest position is not knowing.

studies.title: Say Peace To Them
studies.meaning: The instruction is about a greeting. When believers come, the first words are peace, before anything is taught or corrected. What follows is given as the content of that greeting: mercy is a written commitment, and the conditions attached are unusually gentle. Wrongdoing done in ignorance, then turning back, then repair. The commentators read ignorance broadly, covering anyone who acted without weighing what they were doing, which is most people much of the time.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayat just before describe pressure on the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to send away the poor followers who had nothing to offer, so that the leading men of Mecca could listen without losing face. The refusal of that demand is what this passage follows. The greeting instructed here is addressed to exactly the people he was being asked to dismiss.

keyTerms.note: From a root for wholeness and being free of defect. As a greeting it declares that no harm is intended, and it is the word the Quran uses of the greeting exchanged in the Garden.
Not a lack of information. Commentators explain it as acting without regard for consequence, the state of a person who knew and did not weigh it, which is why the term covers so much ground.

A verb for repairing what has broken, used of mending relations between people. It adds a third step after regret and turning back, and it points outward at the damage rather than inward at the feeling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Greetings in Arabia were social placement. Who you greeted first, whether you greeted at all, and which formula you used declared rank in public. A man of standing was greeted before he greeted, and being passed over was a recognised humiliation. Instructing the Prophet to open with peace towards followers of no consequence inverted a rule everybody watching would have noticed at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about mercy being written appears twice in this surah, and the difference between the two is instructive. At 6:12 it stands inside an argument with opponents about who owns the world. Here it is placed inside a greeting to believers, so the same sentence works once as evidence and once as reassurance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness is described in three moves rather than one: the act, the turning, and the repair. That refuses a version of repentance which is entirely interior. The passage also puts the offer inside a greeting, which changes its register; it is not a warning with a concession attached but news delivered to people already in the room. And the ayah after says that clarity itself exposes the other path.

crossReferences.why: Names the same condition, wrongdoing done in ignorance followed by turning back soon after.
Shows the angels greeting the patient with peace, the same word used here.
Refuses the demand to drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone comes to you with something they have done wrong, notice what your first sentence is. Try making it an ordinary greeting, the kind you would give anyone, before you say anything about the matter. The order in this ayah is deliberate, and it puts the person in the room before the problem.

studies.title: I Will Not Follow Your Desires
studies.meaning: Two statements are given, and the second is the sharper of them. The first reports a prohibition received, so the refusal is not personal preference. The second names what would actually be followed if he complied, and it is not their gods but their desires, which commentators read as identifying the real source of the practice. The closing clause is conditional and unsparing: were he to do it, he would be among the lost, with no exemption claimed for his office.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a period when compromise was being explored. Proposals of shared worship, alternating between his God and theirs, are recorded in the classical sources as part of the negotiation the city attempted before it turned to pressure. This ayah belongs to a family of answers given across several Meccan surahs, all of them refusing the arrangement in similar terms.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb, so the speaker reports rather than decides. The construction places the refusal outside his own judgement, which is why the sentence carries no argument to be negotiated with.
The plural of a word for what a self leans toward, from a root meaning to fall. It names appetite rather than belief, which reclassifies the whole practice being defended.
A participle for those who have found and are following a way. Its use in a conditional sentence about himself removes any suggestion that guidance, once given, cannot be walked away from.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian religion was accommodating by design. Tribes absorbed each other's gods, sanctuaries hosted images from several regions, and adding a deity cost nothing. That flexibility was a practical asset for a city living on visitors. Against that background a refusal to include anything was not read as principle. It was read as bad manners with commercial consequences.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for desires is the same one the Quran elsewhere uses when it describes someone taking his own inclination as a god. Placing it in an argument about idols moves the discussion inward: what is being worshipped, on this account, is finally the self's preference rather than the object it settles on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the alternative to God not in rival deities but in appetite, which is why the refusal cannot be settled by a compromise about names. It also places the speaker under the same terms as everyone else. He states what would happen to him if he yielded, in the same words used of others, so the message is shown to bind its bearer first and to offer him no separate standing.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same refusal its fullest form, separating two ways of worship without hostility.
Names the underlying condition: taking one's own desire as the god one actually serves.
Repeats the declaration in similar words, adding what he does worship instead of what he will not.

studies.applyIt: Think of a preference of yours that you have quietly promoted into a principle: a routine, a taste, a way things ought to be done. Name it accurately for what it is, just once. This ayah's move is to relabel desires honestly, and doing that on something small makes the larger version easier to spot later.

studies.title: The Decision Is Not Mine
studies.meaning: The reply distinguishes two things that were being confused. He stands on clear evidence from his Lord, and that they have rejected. What they are demanding, the punishment they keep asking him to produce, is not his to give. Commentators note the exactness of the wording: not that it will not come, but that it is not in his possession. Judgement is then placed where it belongs, with a God described as one who narrates the truth and separates cases.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the demand behind it recurs through the surah, sometimes as a challenge and sometimes as a taunt. Asking a warner to produce the warning was a way of showing an audience that nothing followed from ignoring him. The classical sources treat the exchange as characteristic of the period rather than tying this ayah to any single day or speaker.

keyTerms.note: Something that makes a matter plain, used in Arabic for legal evidence. The word claims clarity rather than persuasion, which is why the sentence goes straight on to note that it was rejected anyway.
A form meaning to demand that something be brought forward. It names impatience as a request, and the Quran uses it repeatedly of people asking for exactly what they would not want to arrive.
From a root meaning to cut apart. A judge in this vocabulary is one who separates a tangle into its parts, so deciding is pictured as clarifying rather than as choosing a side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in Mecca went to arbitrators, respected men whose work was to divide a tangled matter into parts everyone could see. Their authority came from being trusted to separate rather than to favour, and a well-known arbitrator's ruling could hold across tribes. The word used here for God belongs to that role, and the audience would have heard a familiar profession being invoked.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing what God does with the truth in this ayah is the same one used for telling a story, and it is the root of the Quranic word for narrative. Some early readers of the text read the verb slightly differently, giving the sense of deciding rather than recounting, and the classical commentaries record both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a firm line between bearing a message and controlling its consequences, which protects both the messenger and the audience from a false transaction. It also describes judgement in an unexpected way. Rather than a verdict handed down, it is truth narrated and a tangle separated, so the day of decision is presented as a day when things are finally described accurately.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the same phrase about standing on clear evidence from one's Lord, in another Meccan argument.
Answers the same impatience: the punishment would have arrived already, but for an appointed term.
States the same principle in the middle of a story, that judgement belongs to God alone.

studies.applyIt: Notice a place where you have been carrying responsibility for an outcome that was never yours to decide: a verdict, a diagnosis, another person's choice. Say to yourself, in one sentence, what part is actually in your hands. Then do that part today and leave the sentence where it is. This ayah is a model of the division.

studies.title: The Matter Would Be Settled
studies.meaning: The reply is a conditional that quietly reverses the demand. Had the punishment been in his hands, it would already have come, and the argument between them would be over. Commentators read this as an observation about what human control would have produced: a messenger with power over consequences would have used it, and the delay they treat as weakness is precisely what has kept them alive. The closing clause moves the assessment of who is wronging whom out of the conversation entirely.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the second of two consecutive answers to the same taunt. The community around the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was being harassed and had every human reason to want a decisive intervention. Both ayat say the same thing from different directions: the timing does not belong to him. No specific occasion is reported for either.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb for a matter concluded and closed. The same form appears earlier in this surah about an angel's arrival, so the two answers to two demands are given in identical words.
A word covering a command, a situation and a decision at once. Its breadth here lets one phrase name the whole dispute between the two sides and the verdict that would end it.

A comparative form used absolutely, so it names knowledge beyond anyone's rather than merely greater knowledge. It withdraws the question of who is in the wrong from human assessment, including the speaker's.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blood disputes in Arabia were settled by men who had the power to act and chose when. A clan that could strike and did not was making a decision every day it waited, and everyone understood that restraint under provocation was a position, not an absence. The audience for this ayah knew exactly how to read a delay held by someone with the means to end it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the matter being settled appears twice in this surah within fifty ayat, once about sending an angel and once here about hastening punishment. Both times it answers a demand for something decisive, and both times the answer is that the decisive thing would leave no room for anyone to still be standing there arguing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Delay is presented as a form of mercy rather than as an absence of power, which changes how a quiet heaven should be read. The passage also protects the messenger from an office nobody could hold well. A human being with the ability to call down consequences on his opponents would be a danger, and the ayah says so by simply describing what would have happened. Restraint is located with God, deliberately.

crossReferences.why: States the same point: if God hastened harm as people hasten good, their term would already be over.
Records the taunt in its boldest form, asking for stones from the sky if this is really the truth.
Says that if God held people to account for what they earn, no creature would be left on the earth.

studies.applyIt: Think of a moment when you had the power to end an argument by saying the one thing that would have finished the other person, and did not. Remember what that restraint cost and what it preserved. Then find the smaller version of it today. This ayah treats withheld force as a kindness, which is easiest to believe when you have practised it.

studies.title: The Keys Of The Unseen
studies.meaning: The image is of keys, held by one holder, to what nobody else can open. Then the description narrows instead of expanding, which is the ayah's method: from land and sea, to a single falling leaf, to a seed underground in the dark, to whatever is moist or dry. The commentators note the movement from the vast to the negligible. What ends the sentence is not knowledge but a record, so nothing observed is left unwritten.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah largely occupied with people who wanted proof and with the limits of what human beings can establish for themselves. The ayat around it describe God taking souls at night and returning them by day. The commentators record no occasion for this one, and read it as part of the surah's sustained argument about the difference between what people know and what they assume.

keyTerms.note: The plural can be read as keys or as treasuries, and the classical commentators record both. Either way the point is access: what stands behind them cannot be reached without the one who holds them.
What is absent from perception, not what is mysterious in itself. The word is relative to the observer, which is why the ayah has to add that only He knows these particular things.
The singular form with its feminine ending names one individual leaf rather than foliage in general. That grammatical choice is what makes the example small enough to do the work the sentence needs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: For farmers and herders the buried seed was the standing image of uncertainty. You put grain into dark ground and waited months with no way of knowing what had happened to it, and a season's food hung on that hidden interval. The ayah names exactly that, along with the wet and the dry, the two words a desert people used to divide everything that grows.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah is one of a small group in the Quran built entirely as a descending list, moving from the widest category to the smallest without a break. It contains no command and no address to the listener, and it is among the passages classical commentators return to when discussing what is meant by the clear record named at its end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Divine knowledge is described through the trivial rather than the impressive, which is the harder claim to make. Knowing the count of the stars would be a lesser statement than knowing about one leaf, because the leaf falls beneath the threshold at which anything would normally be recorded. That lands in two directions at once: nothing a person suffers is beneath notice, and nothing done quietly goes unregistered either.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the claim about the smallest weight, in earth or heaven, being in a clear record.
Lists specific things kept with God alone, naming keys this ayah leaves unopened.
Insists that no atom's weight escapes Him, answering those who deny the Hour.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been doing that nobody has noticed: a repeated kindness, a restraint no one sees, a difficulty you have not mentioned. Let this ayah be about that rather than about the universe for a moment. It is built out of the smallest examples available, and that appears to be the point of it.

studies.title: He Takes You By Night
studies.meaning: The verb used for what happens at night is the one the Quran uses for death, and commentators take that seriously: sleep is described as a smaller version of the same event. The daily cycle then becomes a rehearsal. Something is taken, what was done in the light is recorded, and the person is raised again into the same day, until the count of days runs out. The final clause names what the whole sequence is heading toward, which is being told what you did.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage arguing for resurrection with people who accepted a creator and rejected an afterlife. The argument here does not appeal to power or to earlier peoples. It points instead at something the audience did every night, which the surah uses because it cannot be denied and cannot be attributed to anyone else.

keyTerms.note: A verb meaning to receive something in full, used of collecting a debt paid completely. The Quran uses it for death and, here, for sleep, which is why the tradition links the two states.
Literally to wound or cut, and by extension to earn with the hands. The physical sense stays audible, so the day's actions are described with a word that also means leaving a mark.
To give weighty news, from the root behind the word for a prophet's tidings. The final act is telling rather than punishing, which places accurate information at the end of the sequence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sleep was more exposed then than now. People slept on roofs in summer, in tents on the road, and in houses without locks, and a traveller took his rest in the open with animals nearby. Handing over consciousness in that setting was an act of trust performed nightly. Nobody needed persuading that sleep was a state you did not control and did not guarantee waking from.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the same verb for sleep and for death in more than one place, and one passage states directly that God takes souls both at death and during sleep, returning some and retaining others. Arabic therefore has no need of a metaphor here. The two events are described by the identical word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Resurrection is argued from something ordinary rather than from something spectacular, which is characteristic of this surah. If consciousness can be withdrawn and restored nightly by an agency you have no part in, the objection to its being restored once more loses its force. The passage also sets the record and the raising in the same sentence, so the day's actions and the eventual account are shown as one continuous process.

crossReferences.why: States the pairing explicitly: God takes souls at death, and those not dead during their sleep.
Calls sleep a repose and the daytime a rising, using the vocabulary of resurrection for waking.
Offers sleep at night and seeking provision by day as a sign for those who listen.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, notice the last moment you are aware of before sleep, and tomorrow notice the first moment you are aware of after it. You do not manage the gap. Doing this once turns an automatic thing into an observed one, which is exactly the move this ayah makes with a night everybody has already had thousands of times.

studies.title: Envoys Who Never Fail
studies.meaning: A life is described as accompanied from beginning to end. Guardians are sent over a person, and when death arrives it is not an event that happens but an errand carried out by envoys who do not fall short. Commentators note the plural and discuss whether it names a company or those who assist, without settling it. The second ayah closes the circuit: they are returned to their true Master, and the judging belongs to Him, reckoned faster than anyone could count.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and part of a sustained passage on God's authority that opens with the same clause used earlier in this surah. The audience believed in unseen beings and in fate, but not in a recorded life answered for afterwards. These ayat take the unseen company they already accepted and give it a job description that leads somewhere.

keyTerms.note: A plural from the root for preserving and memorising. The same word covers guarding a person and keeping a record, so protection and documentation are named by one term.
The same word used for prophets sent to peoples. Applying it to those who come at death frames the moment as a delivery of a message rather than an interruption of a life.

A word for the one who holds authority and also gives protection, used in Arabia of a freed slave's former owner who remained his ally. Qualified as true, it distinguishes real patronage from the arranged kind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan of value travelled with hired guards, and their reliability was the whole question. Everyone had heard of escorts who slept, ran, or were bought. Payment, reputation and family were staked on it, and a guard who failed once did not work again. The phrase saying these envoys never fall short is drawn straight from that anxiety and answers it in four words.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for guardians comes from the root that also gives the Arabic term for someone who has committed the Quran to memory. Preservation of a text and preservation of a person are described with the same letters, which is why the language of keeping runs through both subjects in the tradition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Death is presented as a collection rather than an ending, carried out by agents under instruction, which removes both randomness and terror from the picture without softening it. The passage also joins two ideas the audience kept apart: an unseen world, which they accepted, and accountability, which they did not. Once the guardians are recorders, the unseen becomes continuous with the reckoning rather than decorative around it.

crossReferences.why: Names the same watchers as noble recorders who know exactly what a person does.
Places two receivers at each side, with nothing uttered but an observer is ready for it.
Answers the same question about death by naming the one charged with taking each person.

studies.applyIt: Choose one ordinary hour today, perhaps your commute, and go through it as though everything in it were being noted, without changing anything for show. Notice how much of that hour you would describe differently afterwards. The passage says a record is kept whether or not you attend to it. Attending to one hour is enough to feel the difference.

studies.title: Humbly And In Secret
studies.meaning: Two adverbs carry the ayah. The calling described is done in lowliness and in hiding, which commentators read as prayer nobody else witnesses, made when there is no audience to perform for. The vow attached is quoted in full, with its promise of thankfulness. Then the answer arrives in two moves: God is the one who delivers, and not only from this but from every distress, and the pattern that follows the rescue is stated without comment. You go back to what you were doing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to traders whose lives involved regular exposure to open desert and to sea crossings from the Arabian coast. The surah has already asked what they would call on in an emergency. Here it moves from the hypothetical to the remembered, describing something the audience had done rather than something they might do. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: Plural again, as at the opening of this surah. Applied to land and sea together, it covers night, storm cloud and depth at once, naming every condition in which a traveller cannot see a way out.

Concealment, from a root for hiding something away. Paired with humility, it describes prayer stripped of any audience, which is why the tradition treats this phrase as a description of sincere calling.
A word for grief that presses on the chest and constricts breathing. It names the bodily feeling of crisis rather than the crisis itself, which is what the promise of deliverance is attached to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravans lost people. A man who wandered from the line at night, a party that missed a well by a few miles, a sandstorm that erased the track: these were ordinary risks, not stories. Sea crossings to Africa and up the Red Sea added their own. Almost every family had someone who had prayed in one of those situations and come home to tell about it.
studies.didYouKnow: Both adverbs in this ayah, humility and secrecy, appear together once more in the Quran, at the start of the next surah, in an instruction about how to call on God. The description of what frightened people already do is thereby turned into the recommended shape of prayer at any time at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies the most honest prayer a person makes and locates it in crisis, which is both a compliment and an indictment. Nothing is wrong with the calling itself; the failure is what follows it. Gratitude is therefore presented not as a feeling at the moment of rescue, which everybody has, but as something that has to survive the return to ordinary conditions, where nothing is pressing on the chest.

crossReferences.why: Asks who answers the one in distress when he calls, and removes the harm afflicting him.
Names the same reflex: every blessing is from God, and to Him you cry when harm arrives.
Shows the prayer from inside the darkness itself, and the deliverance from distress that answered it.

studies.applyIt: Recall a specific time you were rescued from something and remember what you promised while it was happening. Most of us made a promise. Write down the one you made, in the words you used, and do the smallest piece of it this week. The passage does not fault the prayer. It notices what happened after the danger passed.

studies.title: The Violence Of One Another
studies.meaning: Three possibilities are named and the third is the longest. Something from above, something from beneath the feet, or a splitting of the people into parties who are made to taste each other's force. Commentators note that the first two are events and the third is a condition, and that the passage spends most of its words on it. The closing comment repeats a line used earlier in the surah about the signs being turned in different directions, so that they might grasp them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the audience was a city held together by a fragile balance of clans. Mecca had no ruler and no standing force; it worked because rival families found it profitable to cooperate around a sanctuary. Everyone listening had heard of towns and tribes destroyed from within by feud. The third possibility named here was the one they had actually seen.

keyTerms.note: Groups formed around a following, from a root meaning to spread or to follow. The plural describes a body that has separated into camps, each with its own allegiance, rather than a simple disagreement.
From the root for clothing, so the sense is of things becoming entangled and hard to tell apart. Applied to a community, it names the state where nobody can say clearly what the quarrel is.

The causative of tasting, used through the Quran for consequence experienced first hand. Here what is tasted is supplied by other people, which makes the affliction one a community administers to itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian feuds ran for generations. A killing in one season produced an answering killing in the next, and the accounting could continue past the point where anyone remembered the original grievance. The long war between two tribes near Medina had exhausted both sides within living memory. Listeners did not have to imagine a community tasting its own violence; they could name the families involved.
studies.didYouKnow: The comment closing this ayah about turning the signs in different directions appears twice in this surah within twenty ayat, once ending in a note that they still turn away and once, here, in the hope that they will understand. The same clause is given two different endings, which is itself an example of what it describes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Internal division is listed alongside disasters from the sky and from the ground as something of the same order, which raises the stakes on how a community treats itself. The passage does not present factions as a lesser problem handled by people while the real events come from elsewhere. It also leaves the whole list in the conditional. What is being described is capacity, and the point of describing it is understanding rather than fear.

crossReferences.why: Gives the counterpart instruction: hold to God's rope together and do not scatter into separate parties.
Names the same fracturing, of those who split their religion and each faction rejoicing in its own.
Warns that quarrelling among themselves is what drains a community's strength away.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group you belong to that is quietly dividing: a family, a workplace, a community. Identify the one conversation nobody is having because everyone assumes someone else should start it. You do not have to solve anything. Ask one person in the other camp what they actually think, and listen to the whole answer.

studies.title: I Am Not Your Keeper
studies.meaning: The rejection is stated plainly and so is the fact it does not alter: your people denied it, and it is the truth. Then the burden is set down. He is not a keeper over them, which commentators explain as a release from responsibility for outcomes rather than from the work of delivering the message. The second ayah adds the only thing left to say about timing. Every piece of news has a settled place where it comes to rest, and you will know it then.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, after a run of ayat describing what God is able to do and what the listeners keep refusing. This is where the surah turns and speaks to the one carrying the message rather than to those declining it. The classical sources do not report an occasion. The phrase about his own people has weight in a city where the objectors were relatives and neighbours.

keyTerms.note: The agent who manages another's affairs and answers for them. Denying the role removes both the authority to compel and the liability for the result, which are two halves of one office.
News that carries consequence, the same word used earlier in this surah for what will reach those who mocked. Its reappearance ties this promise back to that one.
A noun of place and time from the verb to settle. It can name where something comes to rest or when, and the ambiguity lets the phrase cover both without choosing between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A trusted agent was a real position in Meccan commerce. A merchant travelling north left someone with authority over his goods, his debts and his household, and that man answered for what happened in his absence. The role carried power and exposure together. To say he is not that for them told the audience precisely which relationship was not on offer.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a settled resting place in this ayah appears elsewhere in the Quran for the earth as a dwelling and for the sun's course, so it belongs to the vocabulary of things reaching their appointed position. Applied to news, it treats a report as something travelling toward a location rather than merely being true or false.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is divided cleanly: the message is delivered, the response belongs to those receiving it, and the timing belongs to God. That division is what makes long, unrewarded work sustainable, and the Quran gives it to a messenger before giving it to anyone else. The second ayah adds the piece that makes trust possible, which is that resolution is located rather than merely promised. It has somewhere to arrive.

crossReferences.why: Draws the same line: whoever is guided is guided for himself, and he is not a keeper over them.
States the limit of the office in two clauses: you are a reminder, and not one who controls them.
Repeats the release if they turn away, since he was not sent as a guardian over them.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you have been carrying that belongs to someone else: a decision, a habit, a life you cannot live for them. Say the sentence out loud, that you are not the keeper of this. Then name the one part that is genuinely yours and do that. Setting a thing down properly requires knowing what remains in your hands.

studies.title: Until They Change The Subject
studies.meaning: The instruction is unusually practical. When people are wading into talk about God's signs, withdraw, and the condition for returning is stated exactly: until they move to another topic. Commentators note that no argument is prescribed and no confrontation. Then a provision is made for forgetting, which assumes it will happen. The second ayah relieves the withdrawing person of any account for the others, and gives the whole instruction a purpose that is about them rather than against them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the setting is social rather than formal. Mockery of the recitation happened in gatherings where believers were present, sometimes as entertainment.
